At midnight, the city’s oldest bakery opened one final time. Its sign, faded beyond reading, suddenly illuminated in warm gold, and the locked door swung inward as if surprised by its own obedience. Inside, counters held impossible delicacies: clouds folded into croissants, rain compressed into glossy candies, and one small, trembling pie filled with the scent of childhood.

I entered because I had lost something, though I couldn’t remember what. The baker was an enormous woman made of flour, cinnamon, and patience. She asked no questions. Instead, she placed a plain bun on the counter and waited.

“What was lost?” I asked.

“Everything becomes bread eventually,” she replied. “Even sorrow. Even numbers. Even the names we use for things we cannot say.”

I took the bun. It was warm. In its crust, I saw a street I had never visited, a door I had always wanted to knock on, and my own face looking younger and braver. Then I bit it, and tasted butter, ocean air, and the precise happiness of a summer afternoon with no shadow in sight.

Outside, dawn had begun without permission. The bakery dissolved into brick and glass, but the bun remained in my hand, heavy with possibility.

That morning, I did not recover what I had lost. Instead, I discovered that loss is sometimes merely a place waiting for a different direction. The oven clicked off. The city stirred. Somewhere, a kettle whistled.

And in my pocket, the last crumb whispered: tomorrow was not empty.
